Define residuals, and connect them to the idea of variation in $Y$. - Understand how the least squares method chooses a regression line. - Partition variation into model and error (ANOVA), and use it to compute $R^2$ and RMSE. ## Last time {.smaller} - A **residual** is the leftover gap between an observed value and the model's prediction: $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$. - The **least squares method** picks $\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1$ to minimize $\sum e_i^2$. - Can decompose total variation (SST) into variation explained by the model (SSM) and leftover variation (SSE). ## Empty Model (Mean) vs. Temperature Model Consider the following two models: ::::{.columns} :::{.column} This model just predicts the mean and is called the **empty model** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mean_model <- lm(count ~ NULL, data = fall) mean_model |> tidy() |> kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 4728.163| 127.3915| 37.1152| 0| ::: ::: ::: :::{.column} This model uses `temp_orig` as a predictor and we'll call it the **temperature model** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} temp_model <- lm(count ~ temp_orig, data = fall) temp_model |> tidy() |> kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------|---------:|---------:|---------:|--------:| |(Intercept) | 2077.4771| 475.67243| 4.367453| 2.14e-05| |temp_orig | 152.8729| 26.58745| 5.749815| 0.00e+00| ::: ::: ::: :::: - Which model do you expect to have the smaller SSE? - Which model will explain more variation in `count`? ## Let's think about variation {.smaller} :::{.incremental} - DATA = MODEL + ERROR - $\substack{\text{Total Variation} \\ \text{in Y}} = \substack{\text{Variation explained} \\ \text{by model}} + \substack{\text{Variation not explained} \\ \text{by model}}$ - $SST = SSM + SSE$ (Note, you may see other acronym like $SSR$ instead of $SSE$) - $SST$ = Sum of Squares Total (same as SSE if we use the empty model) - $SSE$ = Sum of Squares Error (the amount of variation not explained by the model) - $SSM$ = Sum of Squares Model (the amount of variation explained by the model) - We've calculated both the $SST$ and $SSE$... we can get the SSM using subtraction: $SST = SSM + SSE$ - Every point's residual is a leftover piece of variation the model didn't explain. ::: ## Putting it all together ::::{.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} augment(temp_model) |> select(count, .fitted, .resid) |> head(3) |> kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | count| .fitted| .resid| |-----:|--------:|----------:| | 2395| 5895.607| -3500.6073| | 5423| 5879.938| -456.9379| | 5010| 6052.302| -1042.3021| ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Compute the SST, SSM, and SSE for using the linear regression model and compare it to the same values if using the mean as our model. ::: :::: ## Properties of least squares regression {.smaller} ::: incremental - Passes through the center of mass point, the coordinates corresponding to average $X$ and average $Y$: $\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{Y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{X}$ - Slope has same sign as the correlation coefficient: $\hat{\beta}_1 = r \frac{s_Y}{s_X}$ + $r$: correlation coefficient + $s_Y, s_X$: sample standard deviations of $X$ and $Y$ - Sum of the residuals is zero: $\sum_{i = 1}^n e_i \approx 0$ (sound familiar?) + Intuition: Residuals are "balanced" - The residuals and $X$ values are uncorrelated ::: ## Partitioning Variability (ANOVA) :::{.incremental} - $y_i - \bar{y} = (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}) + (y_i-\hat{y}_i)$ - Square and sum: $\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2 = \sum(\hat{y} - \bar{y})^2 + \sum(y-\hat{y})^2$ - $\substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{Total}} = \substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{model}} + \substack{\text{Sum of squares} \\ \text{error}}$ - $SSTotal = SSModel + SSE$ - $SST = SSM + SSE$ - This process of partitioning variability is called **Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)**: Analysis of Variance - Involves a whole different way of thinking about modeling and experiemental design ::: ## Residuals in R - `augment` function takes a model and a dataset and computes the residuals (`.resid`), fitted values (`.fitted`), and many other useful quantities ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} augment(temp_model, fall) |> kable() |> # ignore below this line kable_styling() |> scroll_box(width = "1000px", height = "300px") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

What should be the minimum and maximum value of $R^2$ based on this information? 2. Do we want $R^2$ to be big or small? ::: ## $R^2$ ::: incremental - Ranges between 0 (terrible predictor) and 1 (perfect predictor) - Has no units - Calculate with `rsq()` from `yardstick` package from earlier using the augmented data or `supernova`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} temp_aug <- augment(temp_model) rsq(temp_aug, truth = count, estimate = .fitted) |> kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |.metric |.estimator | .estimate| |:-------|:----------|---------:| |rsq |standard | 0.1581379| ::: ::: ::: ## Interpreting $R^2$ {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: poll 🗳️ **Discussion** ::: midi The $R^2$ of the model for `count` from `temp_orig` is 15.8%. Which of the following is the correct interpretation of this value? ::: 1. `temp_orig` correctly predicts 15.8% of `count`. 2. 15.8% of the variability in `count` can be explained by `temp_orig`. 3. 15.8% of the variability in `temp_orig` can be explained by `count`. 4. 15.8% of the time `count` can be predicted by `temp_orig`. ::: ## RMSE {.smaller} ::: incremental - **Root mean square error, RMSE**: A measure of the average error (average difference between observed and predicted values of the outcome) $$ RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i = 1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n}} $$ + Sometimes people just care about numerator (SSE) or version without the square-root (MSE) + Sometimes the denominator may something other than $n$ like $n-1$ or $n-k$ instead - Interpretation (kind of): how much does my model miss by, on average. ::: ::: question 1. What should be the minimum and maximum of RMSE? [0 and infinity]{.fragment} 2. What units are RMSE in? [the same units as the response variable]{.fragment} ::: ## RMSE in R {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} yardstick::rmse(temp_aug, truth = count, estimate = .fitted) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 .metric .estimator .estimate 1 rmse standard 1555. ``` ::: ::: - What's with the `yardstick::` before `rmse`? - Sometimes when you load a lot of packages... multiple packages have functions with the same name... - In this case I'm using two packages `yardstick` and a different one called `Metrics` that both have `rmse`. - R will try to just guess which one you want, but if it guesses wrong, you'll get an error. - Be writing `yardstick::rmse` I'm saying "Use the `rmse` function from `yardstick`" - This will likely not be an issue for you, if it is... that is how you solve it! # Back to your coffee truck models ## Your three models {.smaller} Recall from Monday, you fit three models to your own coffee truck data. ::: question Now that you've seen residuals, SSE, $R^2$, and RMSE — which of your three models do you expect to win? Has your prediction from earlier changed? ::: ## Work time ::: appex 📋 [AE 06-07 - Comparing Models with the Coffee Truck](../ae/ae-06-07-coffee-truck-eval.qmd) ::: Complete the remainder of the exercises. ## Quantitative vs. categorical price {.smaller} ::: incremental - `fit_cat`: (`Price` as the explanatory variable) fits a separate mean for each of the 4 price levels — it has more "freedom" to match the data. - `fit_num` (`PriceNum` as the explanatory variable) forces those 4 means onto a single straight line. - Because a line is a *special case* of "4 free means," `fit_cat`'s $R^2$ can never be smaller than `fit_num`'s $R^2$. - So why not always use the categorical version? - It can't predict at a price it hasn't seen, like \$3.50. - It has no single "per dollar" slope to interpret or report. - It uses more parameters to explain (possibly) only a little more variation ::: ## Using the word "Good" - There is no such thing as a "Good" $R^2$ or, especially, RMSE without **context**. - Whether your model is a "Good" model depends on many things: + What are you using your model for? + How good are other models? + **What else was varying in the data you fit it to?** ## Recap {.smaller} - A **residual** is the leftover gap between an observed value and the model's prediction: $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$. - The **least squares method** picks $\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1$ to minimize $\sum e_i^2$. - Can decompose total variation (SST) into variation explained by the model (SSM) and leftover variation (SSE). - Two metrics for evaluating and comparing models: + $R^2$: What proportion of the variation in the response variable is explained by the model? + $RMSE$: How far does my model miss by, on average? - $R^2$ depends on the data it was fit to, not just the true relationship — so it can't be compared across data sets that vary different things.

  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current

  (function () {

      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {

      if (window.jQuery) {

          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
